samples.summary: Offline-copy recovery silently falls back to `fetchWorkspaces()[0]`, which can publish a document's content into a shared team workspace the user does not own
samples.evidence:
`destinationWorkspace(undefined)` (offline-copy-recovery.ts:174-184) resolves to `(await fetchWorkspaces())[0]?.id` whenever the caller has no `workspaceId`. That branch is reached from `offline-runtime.tsx:271` whenever `fetchDocument(described.id)` answers 404 — i.e. the source document was deleted upstream, which the design names as one of the three ways an archive comes to exist at all.

The archive is a full snapshot of a CRDT document that lived in workspace A. `GET /workspaces` is `workspaceService.findAllByUser(userId)` (see packages/backend/src/datasource/datasource.controller.ts:91 for the same call), which returns *every* workspace the user is a member of — including shared team workspaces, in whatever order the query yields. So the recovered copy, carrying workspace A's document content verbatim, is created in an arbitrary workspace B via `createWorkspaceDocument` (offline-copy-recovery.ts:225,242), where every other member of B can then read it.

Attacker/impact chain: no attacker is needed — a user clicks "Save a copy" on the toast (offline-runtime.tsx:285), the toast says only `Recovered as "<title>"` (offline-runtime.tsx:304) and never names the destination, and confidential content from a deleted private workspace lands in a workspace shared with colleagues. The user is given no opportunity to choose or even observe the destination before the write.

The design (docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md) justifies the fallback as "handing the work back somewhere beats refusing", but does not address that "somewhere" may be a multi-member workspace. Refusing, or prompting for a destination, would be the safe direction.

samples.summary: An expired session (401) leaves full local document content and its client-key salts on a shared device for up to 30 days, and the design's stated mitigations do not cover it
samples.evidence:
`fetchWithAuth`'s 401 arm passes `eraseLocalData: "none"` (api/auth.ts:275), so `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout()` never runs. It also never calls `rememberOfflineUser(undefined)`, so `wafflebase-offline-user` keeps naming the departed account and no pending-erase marker is recorded (`offline-erase.ts:310-347` is the only writer of `PENDING_ERASE_KEY`).

The result on the shared machine this feature is explicitly built for: user A's complete gzip'd document snapshots stay in IndexedDB, and their per-document client-key salts stay in `localStorage` under `wafflebase-durable-device:{A}:{docKey}` (durable-session.ts:157). `localStorage` and IndexedDB are origin-scoped, so user B — the next person to sign in on that browser profile, with devtools — can read both. `durable-session.ts:120-128` concedes exactly this ("It does not defend against somebody sitting at this browser profile").

The three mitigations the design names do not close it. (1) The deliberate sign-out did not happen — that is the premise. (2) The "reconcile the next session runs" is `purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments`, which scopes to `offlineUserId()` and `store.storedDocumentIds()` under `this.userId` (offline-erase.ts:469-489) — running as user B it touches only B's rows and never reaches A's. (3) That leaves only `collectStale`'s thirty-day sweep, i.e. a 30-day exposure window of full document text to a co-user of the machine.

A session that simply expires is by far the commonest way one ends on a borrowed or lab machine, so this is the modal case rather than an edge one. A narrower policy — dropping snapshots while keeping only entries whose change log is non-empty — would preserve the unsent-work argument the 401 skip rests on without retaining whole documents.

samples.summary: `purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments` returns 0 without throwing when no identity is recorded, which the caller reads as a successful reconcile and uses to open the archive-recovery gate
An identity change under a mounted durable client re-mounts the previous user's in-memory document under the new user's client key and IndexedDB store scope
samples.evidence:
`subject = `${person?.id ?? 'anon'}:${docKey}`` (collab-document-provider.tsx:256) deliberately re-decides when the identity changes, and `person` tracks the latest resolved `['me','optional']` (line 215). React Query refetches on window focus, so on a shared browser: user A has `/s/7` open with a durable client; user B signs in in another tab; tab A's `me` resolves to B; `subject` moves to `2:sheet-7`; `held.current` is replaced (line 270) and a new `DurableYorkieProvider` is mounted with `clientKey={durableClientKey("2", "sheet-7")}` and `userId="2"` (lines 355-356).

The `DocumentProvider` beneath it still carries the Yorkie document hydrated during A's session, and the new store is constructed with `userId: "2"` (durable-yorkie-provider.tsx), so every header/archive row it writes is stamped as B's and is therefore listable by `listArchives()`/`loadArchive()` under B's identity and recoverable by B as a document they own.

What stands between that and an actual cross-account disclosure is entirely server-side: the Yorkie auth webhook rejecting B's personal token for `sheet-7`. There is no client-side check that the new identity may read the document already in memory before the store is attached under their scope. I could not confirm whether the SDK writes any snapshot before the attach is accepted, which is why confidence is low; if it does, this is a direct cross-account content leak into B's store scope.

samples.summary: The path-traversal regression assertion is weakened from "every request URL carries the id encoded" to "at least one does"
samples.evidence:
The old assertion ran `expect(pathname).toContain(encodeURIComponent(TRAVERSAL))` inside the per-URL loop, so every request a call emitted had to carry the id percent-encoded. It is now `paths.some(...)` (url.test.ts:170-174).

For `deleteWorkspace(TRAVERSAL)` the new `documentIdsIn` helper (api/workspaces.ts) calls `fetchWorkspace(ref)` first, and that request *does* contain `encodeURIComponent(TRAVERSAL)` — so the `some(...)` is satisfied by the companion request alone, even if `deleteWorkspace`'s own `DELETE ${BASE}/${seg(id)}` later dropped its `seg()`. The same holds for `removeMember`.

The surviving `not.toContain("/auth/logout")` loop still catches the one payload the suite uses (`"../../auth/logout"`, url.test.ts:68), because that payload normalizes into `/auth/logout...` wherever it is interpolated raw. So this is coverage reduction rather than an open hole: a regression that interpolated a route param raw in a position that does *not* normalize onto `/auth/logout` (a query string, a differently-shaped traversal) would now pass. Asserting `toContain` over every URL that is *supposed* to carry the id — e.g. by filtering out the known id-free companion requests rather than relaxing to `some` — would restore the stronger property.

samples.summary: The client-key salt falls back to `Math.random()` when `crypto.getRandomValues` is absent, and is only 64 bits
samples.evidence:
`randomSecret()` (durable-session.ts:244-257) fills 8 bytes from `crypto.getRandomValues` when available and otherwise from `Math.floor(Math.random() * 256)`. `Math.random()` is not a CSPRNG and its state is recoverable from a handful of outputs in every major engine, so a salt minted that way is derivable — which is exactly the property the salt exists to deny (the file's own comment at lines 80-104 explains that Yorkie authorizes `ActivateClient`/`DeactivateClient` on token validity alone, so a derivable key lets any workspace peer tear down another member's per-document client).

The in-code justification is that the branch is unreachable because `navigator.locks` and `crypto` are both secure-context APIs and `supportsDurableSession()` gates the feature on the former. That holds today, but the coupling is incidental rather than enforced — `supportsDurableSession()` also returns `true` unconditionally whenever a lock manager is injected (line 58). Throwing, or declining durability, would be safer than minting a guessable salt. Separately, 64 bits is on the low side for a value whose whole job is to be unguessable and which is long-lived on disk; 128 bits costs nothing here.

samples.summary: The post-erase write denial and the owed-erase queue are unauthenticated localStorage values, so clearing one key re-enables writes for an account whose data was just erased
samples.evidence:
`isOfflineWritePermitted` (offline-erase.ts:208-213) is the guard that stops a still-mounted durable client from re-writing a signed-out account's document back to disk after `dropAllForUser`. Its authority is `localStorage['wafflebase-offline-denied']` (line 145), read through `deniedIds()` with no integrity check. The same is true of `wafflebase-offline-erase-pending` (line 231), which is the *only* record that an account is still owed an erase, and of `wafflebase-offline-user` (line 62), which is the only thing naming whose data may be erased.

Anyone able to run script on the origin — including the next person to sign in on the shared device this feature targets, via devtools — can `localStorage.removeItem('wafflebase-offline-denied')` to lift the denial, or `removeItem('wafflebase-offline-erase-pending')` so the owed erase from a failed sign-out is silently dropped and the departed account's documents stay on the disk until the thirty-day sweep.

This is inherent to a client-side control and is not remotely exploitable, so it is hardening rather than a break — but the module's doc comment presents the localStorage move as what makes the denial reach "as far as the writers do", and it is worth recording that the control is tamperable by exactly the local actor the feature's threat model names.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described and is reachable. `destinationWorkspace` (offline-copy-recovery.ts:174-184) falls back to `(await fetchWorkspaces())[0]?.id` with no ownership/membership-role filter and no ordering guarantee; it is consumed at offline-copy-recovery.ts:226 and :243 as the target of `createWorkspaceDocument`, followed by writing the archived CRDT content into it. The undefined-workspace path is reached from offline-runtime.tsx:266-278, where a 404 from `fetchDocument` is deliberately swallowed and `workspaceId` is left undefined, then passed to `recoverOfflineCopy` at offline-runtime.tsx:287-291 when the user clicks "Save a copy". `fetchWorkspaces` (api/workspaces.ts:41-45) is served by `workspaceService.findAllByUser` (workspace.service.ts:32-38), a `workspaceMember.findMany({ where: { userId } })` with no `orderBy` and no owner-only filter, so index 0 can be any shared team workspace. The success toast (offline-runtime.tsx:304) never names the destination, so the write happens without the user seeing or choosing where confidential content landed. No guard elsewhere constrains the fallback; this is sensitive-data exposure to other workspace members and falls squarely in the security lane.

verdict.reason: The reviewer's factual claims all check out: auth.ts:277 does pass eraseLocalData:"none", logout()'s gate at auth.ts:134 skips eraseOfflineDataOnLogout(), the 401 path never calls rememberOfflineUser(undefined), offline-erase.ts:310-347 is the only writer of PENDING_ERASE_KEY, and purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments (offline-erase.ts:468-489) scopes to offlineUserId() so it never reaches a departed account's rows. So `not-present` and `already-guarded` do not apply. It is nonetheless not blocking under the Security rubric. (1) No permission gate, signature check, or auth path is bypassed or weakened; this is a data-retention policy for an at-rest store the user opted into, with an explicitly documented competing harm — fetchWithAuth is the funnel every request goes through, so any background 401 would erase the open document's un-pushed change log (auth.ts:260-277, design doc:180-198, 281-287). (2) The proposed remedy would not close the exposure class: the identical residual exists whenever a session ends with no 401 ever firing — browser closed, machine powered off, tab crashed — cases collectStale's own comment names (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1171-1174) and which no client-side code can ever reach. The 401 arm is therefore not a weak entry point relative to the feature's unavoidable baseline; the ask is a shorter retention window for the whole feature, a product decision. (3) The stated bound genuinely executes and is genuinely cross-account: collectStale sweeps live entries and archives whoever wrote them (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1182-1208) and runs once per session from the shell (offline-runtime.tsx:123), with sweepStaleSecrets doing the same for salts (durable-session.ts:219-230, 283). (4) The salts are not credentials: durable-session.ts:74-105 scopes them to stopping a workspace peer from deriving a client key to deactivate a client row, which still needs the peer's own valid token — no authN/authZ gain for a reader who can already read the same IndexedDB. (5) The adversary holds the browser profile, where the origin model offers no isolation the app can assert, as durable-session.ts:124-128 and the design doc:400-414 both state. That makes this a hardening suggestion about a documented, bounded retention window — minor/nit under this lens's severity definitions, not an exploitable vulnerability or a broken security control.

finding.summary: `purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments` returns 0 without throwing when no identity is recorded, which the caller reads as a successful reconcile and uses to open the archive-recovery gate

verdict.reason: The quoted code exists, but the state it needs is guarded into harmlessness. (1) The caller sets the module identity synchronously as the first statement of the same effect (offline-runtime.tsx:66 -> offline-erase.ts:75-82), and purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments reads offlineUserId() as its first synchronous statement (offline-erase.ts:469) with no await between the cancelled check (offline-runtime.tsx:156) and that read, so no interleaving is possible at the call site. (2) rememberOfflineUser(undefined) has only two call sites, both inside eraseOfflineDataOnLogout (offline-erase.ts:313, 337), reachable only from a user-chosen, server-confirmed logout (auth.ts:134-136); line 337 runs only after `await eraseOfflineData(store, who)` succeeded (offline-erase.ts:332), and that erase drops the user's live entries AND every archive (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1140-1163). So whenever the falsy branch is taken, the disk already holds nothing for that identity — listArchives is user-scoped (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1062-1067) and feeds listRecoverableWork (offline-copy.ts:58-68), which would return empty. (3) The claimed impact (materializing an archive as a new server document owned by the signed-in user) requires an authenticated session, which the only precondition destroys: fetchDocument routes through fetchWithAuth (documents.ts:46-50), whose 401 arm throws AuthExpiredError (auth.ts:255-281), which is not an HttpError 404, so offline-runtime.tsx:271-276 takes `continue` and no offer is ever rendered; recoverOfflineCopy could not create a document either. In any authenticated session the identity is non-empty, so the branch is not taken at all. The residual is a semantically wrong boolean in a window where nothing is left on disk and no session exists to act on it — not a reachable authorization bypass or data exposure under the security rubric.

finding.summary: An identity change under a mounted durable client re-mounts the previous user's in-memory document under the new user's client key and IndexedDB store scope
finding.evidence:
`subject = `${person?.id ?? 'anon'}:${docKey}`` (collab-document-provider.tsx:256) deliberately re-decides when the identity changes, and `person` tracks the latest resolved `['me','optional']` (line 215). The `DocumentProvider` beneath it still carries the Yorkie document hydrated during A's session, and the new store is constructed with `userId: "2"` (durable-yorkie-provider.tsx), so every header/archive row it writes is stamped as B's and is therefore listable by `listArchives()`/`loadArchive()` under B's identity and recoverable by B as a document they own.

What stands between that and an actual cross-account disclosure is entirely server-side: the Yorkie auth webhook rejecting B's personal token for `sheet-7`. There is no client-side check that the new identity may read the document already in memory before the store is attached under their scope. I could not confirm whether the SDK writes any snapshot before the attach is accepted, which is why confidence is low; if it does, this is a direct cross-account content leak into B's store scope.

verdict.reason: The finding's mechanism requires the DocumentProvider (holding A's hydrated Yorkie doc) to stay mounted while the DurableYorkieProvider above it swaps to B's clientKey/store. That cannot happen: on the render where `person` moves A->B, `useDurableDocument` is called with the new userId, its subject changes (use-durable-document.ts:186), `answered` is false because `decision` is only set from an effect (use-durable-document.ts:192-232), so `settled` is false (use-durable-document.ts:254) and `ready` is false (collab-document-provider.tsx:268). `held.current` is therefore not replaced on that render (the guard at :269 requires `ready`), and the pre-decision gate at collab-document-provider.tsx:333-335 returns null, unmounting DurableYorkieProvider and the entire DocumentProvider subtree. Only after B's election settles does a fresh DocumentProvider mount under B's client key, against an empty `wb:…:{B}:{docKey}` store scope — so no content hydrated in A's session is written or stamped under B's identity. The degenerate case where `ready` is true at the transition (eligible false, e.g. preference off) switches to the bare `inner` element, a different element type at the same position, which also unmounts the subtree and mounts no store at all. The repo's own test confirms the null frame: collab-document-provider-durable.test.tsx:173-199 flips the identity 7->9 and asserts exactly one recorded provider render under the old key (no provider render on the transition), in contrast to the preference test at :216-231 which explicitly asserts DOM-node survival. The residual data-loss of A's queue is a correctness concern in the opposite direction, not a cross-account disclosure.

finding.summary: The share-link PDF route mounts CollabDocumentProvider outside NonDurableScope, so the positional share-link durability gate does not cover it
finding.evidence: `SharedDocumentInner` returns `<SharedPdfLayout .../>` at shared-document.tsx:969 — an EARLY RETURN that happens before the `<NonDurableScope>` wrapper added at line 1017. `SharedPdfLayout` (line 753) mounts its own `YorkieProvider` and then `PdfCollabProvider`, which renders `CollabDocumentProvider` (app/files/pdf-collab.tsx:200). `useDurabilityPermitted()` therefore answers its default `true` (use-durable-document.ts:61) on that subtree. Today the route is saved only by the unrelated `isExcluded(docKey)` rule (`docKey.startsWith('pdf-')`, use-durable-document.ts:40-42), which the design states is temporary: docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md says PDF is "excluded until it has a chip". The moment that exclusion is lifted, a signed-in visitor on somebody else's share link gets the durable branch on this route — their own `wb:{salt}:{userId}:pdf-<id>` client authenticating with `fetchYorkieToken` (their personal token) rather than the share token whose role and expiry the auth webhook validates, and the shared document's comment content written to a disk the link's revocation cannot reach. That is precisely the bypass `NonDurableScope` was added to close, and the gate reads as covering the whole share route when it does not. `shared-document-durability.test.tsx` only exercises `resolved.type: 'sheet'`, so no test covers the pdf branch.

verdict.reason: The positional observation is factually correct — SharedPdfLayout is returned early (shared-document.tsx:968-981) before the NonDurableScope wrapper (shared-document.tsx:1017), and NonDurableScope exists nowhere else in packages/frontend/src outside that file and tests — but the operation the gate protects is independently guarded on that exact path, so the described bypass is not reachable. The PDF share route can only mount CollabDocumentProvider with docKey `pdf-${documentId}` (pdf-collab.tsx:200-201); useDurableDocument's eligibility requires `!isExcluded(docKey)` (use-durable-document.ts:127-132) and isExcluded returns true for every `pdf-` key (use-durable-document.ts:40-42); clientKey is undefined unless durable (use-durable-document.ts:249); and the only DurableYorkieProvider mount in the whole app is gated on `decided.durable && decided.clientKey && person` (collab-document-provider.tsx:351-372). So no personal-token durable client is minted, no election is taken and no IndexedDB store is attached for a share-link PDF visitor. This is enforced, not incidental: tests assert it at use-durable-document.test.tsx:134 and collab-document-provider-durable.test.tsx:260-269. The reviewer's chain depends on a hypothetical future lifting of the pdf- exclusion (docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md:112-114), which makes it a defense-in-depth/hardening concern rather than a present authorization weakness or exploitable vector.
